National Parliament
National Assembly
Complete Details of the Twenty-First Session
Proceedings of
Baisakh 39, 2083
Thursday
Meeting Number -
Today's meeting of the National Assembly commenced at 11:19 AM under the chairmanship of the Right Honourable Chairperson Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal.
(11:19 AM)
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable members, the proceedings of the meeting will now commence. Honourable members, names of honourable members have been received to speak during the Zero Hour. I will provide time to the honourable members to speak. Each honourable member has been allocated 1 minute to speak during the Zero Hour. First, Honourable Member Krishna Bahadur Rokaya.
Honourable Mr. Krishna Bahadur Rokaya
(Nepali Congress):- (11:20 AM)
Right Honourable Chairperson Sir, on Baisakh 17, a Bolero jeep traveling from Rukumkot in Rukum East to Jaljala in Rolpa met with an accident in Thabang Rural Municipality Ward No. 1 of Rolpa, resulting in the deaths of 20 people. Subsequently, on Baisakh 29, a passenger bus returning after visiting the Supa Deurali temple in Arghakhanchi's Panche Rural Municipality had an accident at Kurle of Arghakhanchi, resulting in two deaths at the scene and three deaths during treatment, making a total of five deaths. I offer heartfelt condolences to those who lost their lives in both incidents and express deep sympathy to the bereaved families, and wish a speedy recovery to the injured.
Right Honourable Chairperson Sir, both these incidents have once again raised serious questions about road safety in Nepal's hilly regions, technical inspection of vehicles, the tendency to carry more passengers than capacity, and temporary transportation management during pilgrimages and festivals. Government data indicates that an average of eight people lose their lives daily due to road accidents. Drawing the serious attention of the concerned bodies to this, I strongly demand, through the Honourable Chairperson, a response from the relevant ministry regarding the Government of Nepal's plan to prevent such incidents from recurring in the future. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Padam Bahadur Pariyar.
(11:21 AM)
Honourable Mr. Padam Bahadur Pariyar (Nepali Congress):- Right Honourable
(11:21 AM)
Sir, Mr. Deepak Bhandari, who has a complete physical disability, has been protesting to demand personal assistant services as per the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2074. Just yesterday, he wrote a public letter to the Right Honourable Prime Minister stating that either the government should provide the facilities granted by that law, or if it cannot provide them, then grant him the right to euthanasia. He has made this demand. He has expressed a desire to meet the Right Honourable Prime Minister once. Through the Right Honourable Chairperson, I request that the Right Honourable Prime Minister listen to the concerns of this completely disabled individual and also consider his demand for euthanasia. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member Puja Chaudhary.
(11:22 AM)
Honourable Ms. Puja Chaudhary (Janata Samajwadi Party, Nepal):- Right Honourable
(11:22 AM)
Chairperson, the lives of the landless squatters are in disarray. There is no proper arrangement for food, nor for drinking water. Children are in one place and parents in another. There is no clarity about their education, and it is still uncertain when they will be able to attend school. We have also seen the tears of the elderly. Therefore, I urge the government that you have demolished the squatter settlements, but before demolishing the remaining ones, there should first be a proper management arrangement, and only then should the houses of the landless squatters be demolished. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Rukmini Koirala.
(11:23 AM)
Honourable Ms. Rukmini Koirala (Nepal Communist Party, UML):- Right Honourable
(11:23 AM)
Chairperson, regarding the Cooperative Act, 2074 Ordinance, for the spouse, son, daughter-in-law, daughter, son-in-law, adopted son, adopted daughter-in-law, father, mother, stepmother, and elder/younger siblings, uncles, aunts, grandparents, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and self-raised individuals. For female members, mother-in-law and father-in-law are mentioned. This means only the one who consumes it has to repay it, and this is not in international law and is not accepted. It is a violation of human freedom, and blame cannot be placed on others. This is a fight between people, which is and will be unacceptable. I want to draw the government's attention to this and request that this point be amended. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Renu Chand.
(11:24 AM)
Honourable Ms. Renu Chand (Nepali Communist Party):- Right Honourable Chairperson Sir,
(11:24 AM)
I request that arrangements be made for pedestrian entry into Singha Durbar. Not everyone has a vehicle. There are also MPs who use public transport and walk. However, MPs arriving by car have easy entry. It is somewhat inconvenient for MPs arriving on foot. I request that the arrangements for pedestrian movement be made easier. The old path near the south gate should be reopened. I request that it be reopened. Now, if you ask for vehicles, you will be told you don't have them. Then they say MPs are asking for facilities. Please create an environment for walking. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota.
(11:24 AM)
Honourable Ms. Bishnu Kumari Sapkota (Nepali Congress):- Right Honourable Chairperson,
(11:24 AM)
Today, I want to draw the government's serious attention to the problems of landless squatters, unorganized settlers, and genuinely poor citizens across the country. According to the data submitted by the National Land Problem Resolution Committee to the government on Baisakh 4, there are a total of 1,203,519 families of landless Dalits, landless squatters, and unorganized settlers in Nepal. They have been deprived of permanent settlement, basic services, and a dignified life for generations. The Constitution of Nepal guarantees every citizen the right to housing, social justice, and to live with dignity. Therefore, I urge the government to ensure transparent identification of genuine landless individuals, land management or alternative housing, and basic services such as education, health, drinking water, and electricity. If a policy of evicting all citizens without land ownership deeds is implemented, more than 900,000 families of unorganized settlers across the country will be directly affected.
Eviction without management is not a solution. It will create a social and humanitarian crisis. Therefore, my clear plea to the government is, solution first.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma.
(11:26 AM)
Honourable Mr. Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma (Nepali Communist Party):- Right Honourable
(11:27 AM)
Chairperson Sir, Mr. Shrikrishna BK, a resident of SunKoshi Rural Municipality in Sindhuli district, eloped with Nirjala Magar from Khotang district. He reached his home on Baisakh 1, and on Baisakh 4, the Satdobato Police Post summoned him, took him into custody, and then transferred him to the Khotang Area Police Office, where he died in custody. It appears that the young man, who married consensually, was tortured and died in custody on the pretext of alleged rape. Therefore, I demand strict punishment for those who are responsible for this act of not providing security to Dalit youth even within custody. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Shrikrishna Prasad Adhikari.
(11:28 AM)
Honourable Mr. Shrikrishna Prasad Adhikari (Nepali Communist Party):- Right Honourable
(11:28 AM)
Chairperson Sir, the condition of the landless squatters kept in holding centers like Ichchhu Narayan Madhav Ashram is extremely dire. They lack proper drinking water, clothes, and are sick. Children are unable to study, and they have lost their jobs. I want to ask the government when this situation will end. The government is still proceeding with demolishing squatter settlements without any management. I strongly warn this government to stop this inhumane treatment of evicting landless squatters without management. Thank you.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Savitri Malla.
(11:29 AM)
Honourable Ms. Savitri Malla (Nepali Communist Party):- Right Honourable
(11:29 AM)
Sir, I request permission to present my views and suggestions point-wise on the government's policy and program for the fiscal year 2083/084, presented by the Right Honourable President to the joint session of the Federal Parliament on Baisakh 28, 2083. The presented policy and program appear to be traditional and a continuation of the past. No novelty was observed. There was no mention of national pride projects in the policy and program, making it unclear what the government's concept of development is. On one hand, the price hike of petroleum products is increasing the economic value of goods and services in the market. This policy and program are silent on how to provide relief to the public. On the other hand, despite the confirmation of gas excavation in Dailekh, there was no subject matter included in the policy and program regarding production. I did not find any such subject matter in this policy and program.
Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable members, the Zero Hour for honourable members to speak concludes here.
Honourable members, the discussion on the policy and program of the Government of Nepal for the fiscal year 2083/084, mentioned in the address by the Right Honourable President to a joint meeting of both houses of the Federal Parliament on Monday, Baisakh 28, 2083, will continue.
Honourable members, I will provide time sequentially to the remaining honourable members who are scheduled to participate in the discussion based on their party affiliation. First, Honourable Member Chandra Bahadur K.C. Time: 12 minutes. Following this, Honourable Member Jayanti Devi Rai.
Honourable Mr. Chandra Bahadur K.C. (Nepali Congress):- Right Honourable
(11:31 AM)
Chairperson Sir, today, I am here at this rostrum to briefly share my thoughts on the two programs for 2083/084 presented by the Right Honourable President. Firstly, what I feel is that culture is the mother of civilization. Tradition is the foundation upon which it rests. As the Right Honourable President was reading the policy and program, the Right Honourable Prime Minister stood up and left. I feel like asking, where did that culture, that civilization, that tradition go? I want to share this in this house. While efforts have been seen from yesterday to today to find an answer, no success has been achieved. Now, regarding these policies and programs, as they come, they seem to be moving towards breaking old traditions and establishing new ones, laying new foundations, while on one hand, in countries like Britain and Israel, precedents and laws that have been traditionally formed are still working and are being made. But in our country, the current government appears to be moving towards breaking such precedents, old precedents, and traditions, and establishing new needs and precedents.
And along with that, policies and programs have been brought through ordinances by convening the parliament on the eve of the parliamentary session, stopping the parliament, and setting up a stage on the eve of the parliamentary session. When we look for that parliamentary tradition and the parliamentary system followed in the international community, we are asked, the inner self asks, shouldn't we also do some further programs for justice? Therefore, these issues have been raised. The Ministry of Home Affairs is currently vacant. This morning, I heard that the former Finance Minister...

When it comes to listening, the resignation of the Home Minister... happened, but here, the Right Honourable Prime Minister has accepted the resignation of the Home Minister, Suden Gurung, who was previously in office. Even that is not clear yet. Therefore, what is evident now is the Prime Minister's attire, his getup and makeup, in the history of the Prime Minister so far. His attire is unlike anything seen in the history of Nepal. Is it an attempt to add a new dimension to Nepal's history? This is a topic of widespread discussion everywhere. Considering the policy and program brought by the government, within that policy and program, did the Right Honourable Prime Minister, while the Right Honourable President was speaking and walking, did that policy and program... or ex-officio? Since a minister is present here, it has become necessary to mention it, so I am mentioning it. Looking at it, what is evident now is that the parliament is the executive, the executive is made by the parliament, not the parliament by the executive. Therefore, the Prime Minister, as part of the executive, must be accountable and responsible to the parliament. That was not seen yesterday. Ten such incidents have been seen since the first day the policy and program was presented. And on the other hand, looking at it superficially, it seems that instead of being accountable to the parliament, an attempt has been made to impose sanctions on the parliament. Simultaneously, the executive seems to have attacked the judiciary as well. As I said earlier, there are rules based on Britain and tradition. Is it an attempt to break those traditions and establish new ones? This policy and program is also lagging behind previous policies and programs, and has not been able to establish new traditions. This is a contradiction in itself, it seems. And as I looked at the policy and program superficially, I prefer 'Pratantra' over democracy. It uses the word. Therefore, in a federal republic, the people are sovereign. The executive is trying to make the people ignorant and blind. The executive is above the law, the executive is above the constitution. The executive is above the legislature. The executive is above the judiciary. This was clearly demonstrated by the activity of the Right Honourable Prime Minister yesterday in the context of the President's address. Therefore, the sovereign people, who are not ignorant or simple, and know how to find their way, if the government has taken this into account, it should remove the earwax and listen. I feel that the policy and program has come about by cutting branches of a tree, by collecting fallen leaves from the branches. But they are not in a basket. That kind of working paper is the policy and program that has come now. In the working paper, in the policy and program, is there any mention or reference to the amendment or review of the Constitution of Nepal? That is a subject of debate. Although it has been raised in their manifesto, in the manifesto of the Rastriya Swatantra Party, and in the manifesto of the current government, there is no mention or reference to it anywhere in the policy and program. And another issue is that it has not been able to define the relationship and distance between the federal, provincial, and local governments. It has not sought to strengthen it. It has not sought to make laws for it. What is the new thinking about the provinces? What is the promise? Is it the promise written in the manifesto? Or the current additional promise? The policy and program has not shown a tally of both. And simultaneously, if the federal, provincial, and local governments are to be strengthened, the concept of adopting the principle of decentralization is being pursued. It has not been attempted to include it in the current policy and program by explaining and analyzing it. Simultaneously, yesterday I heard in the news that the Election Commission has proposed holding federal and provincial elections simultaneously, on the same day. If that happens, does the government know about it or not? If it is a constitutional body of the government, will that matter come into the policy and program or not? Will it be part of the national agenda or not? The policy and program is silent on this as well. And simultaneously, it is stated that Nepal's GDP growth rate will be 7 percent. The issue of income growth has been raised. But regarding remittance money, a scholar named Sukhdev Shah wrote about it. This remittance money comes in billions and trillions. Is this truly remittance sent by Nepalis who went abroad for honest work, work according to merit, work according to pay, work according to need, for livelihood? Or is there some other backing force behind the billions and trillions of remittances? This needs to be investigated. It is not seen in the manifesto either. It is not included in the current policy and program either. And simultaneously, regarding the balance of trade, trade with India, trade with China, there is a deficit. Where will the compensation for this come from? How will it be done? The policy and program should come as a national policy on this, but it has not. And simultaneously, what is the alternative to remittance money? This is not it. Nothing has been seen about this in the policy and program either. And another issue is that Nepal's labor market is empty, Nepalis are going to foreign labor markets. I am not saying this with any prejudice. It is found that foreign powers, including India, are coming here and working. From stitching shoes to selling fruits, selling vegetables. And the nation is emphasized greatly. But where is national production? Where is the market for the vegetables grown here in Dhading? Why are they thrown on the streets? Why are the vegetables grown in Kaski thrown on the roads? The policy and program should come as a national policy on these issues. It is silent on these matters. And not just the labor market, this policy and program does not speak about the declining population. Perhaps India has developed due to a dense population. Perhaps China has developed due to a dense population. Perhaps Yugoslavia has developed due to a dense population. If we look at Nepal's population statistics, if we look at the recent report of the Central Bureau of Statistics, Nepal's population is not 30 million, it is around 28.8 million. Where did the rest go? If you segment it, I think around 10 million are abroad. There might be 20 million here. 10 million are in the cities. Half of the 10 million might be in the villages. In the villages, people are being harassed by wild animals day and night, with talk of monkeys and tigers coming up. Therefore, a strong, firm policy with economic intent is not seen in this working paper. And simultaneously, regarding the population, this is something that needs to be thought about. My request and appeal to the government that made promises in this manifesto is only this: Nepalis are going abroad in large numbers, marrying between 35 and 40 years of age, and if they have children, they are having only one. From where will the population become dense? Nepalis who have gone abroad are not returning, they are getting married and staying there. Therefore, there is a need for national reflection on this. Why is the population not increasing? Why is it decreasing? It is estimated that Nepal's population will fall to 20 million within the next 10 years. Our Foreign Minister is a scholar. I have also informed him. This is the situation. Nepal's diplomatic sector is in a dire state. And looking at the diplomatic sector, regarding Lipulekh, Limpiyadhura, what is the policy and program with a firm resolve on these matters? It is not seen. And simultaneously, regarding Nepal's diplomatic relations, connecting the world, connecting global politics, connecting global development, there is no clear stance in the policy and program regarding MCC and BRI. Touching is not enough, it should be like touching. Writing is not enough, there should be a resolve and intention to act. In that sense, diplomacy is in a dire state. For many days, the places that have been called, ambassadors are vacant. Even now, if you look, the Ministry of Home Affairs has nine or ten vacant CDO positions. Assistant CDOs are working, some places are being managed by administrative officers. This is the situation in the country. Therefore, it is easy to break, slogans are easy. It is easy to shake social media and shed leaves. But it is difficult to collect, difficult to bring stability. Winning the digital war does not mean winning the war forever. There are other warriors in that digital war. May the government's attention turn to that. And in the word diplomacy, this is it. Now this government talks about Gen Z, Gen Z. Everyone does. I say Gen Z. It's a Western language. I prefer the movement for generational transition. (.. Time is up.) Honourable Chairperson: What is it, Honourable Member? On what? On what subject? On what? (11:44 AM) Honourable Member Padam Bahadur Pariyar (Nepali Congress): (.. Sound not heard.) (11:44 AM) According to Rule 21 of the National Assembly Regulations, it is stipulated that no discriminatory language based on caste, gender, community, or disability shall be used in the assembly. Just now, words like 'blind', 'dumb' people were used in the assembly. These words have insulted the entire disabled community. They have caused disrespect. Therefore, I request that these words be removed from the record and a ruling be made so that such disrespectful language and words are not used in future sessions, Honourable Chairperson. Honourable Chairperson: Honourable Member, where and how were those words used? (11:45 AM) I have instructed the Secretariat to look into it and take it forward in the next meeting. For now, I have given instructions to the Secretariat. Where and how those words were used. Honourable Member, now Jayanti Devi Rai. Time: 6 minutes. After this, Honourable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri. Honourable Member Jayanti Devi Rai (Communist Party of Nepal): Honourable Chairperson, (11:46 AM) Sir, at this time, we are discussing the budget policy and program for 2083 and 2084. This budget policy and program has come with some good aspects and novelty. I would like to welcome it. However, with the strength of a two-thirds government, a new party, new power, new ideas, and a new individual, this program has not met the expectations of the people. We had hoped that the current government would address the issues that the previous government could not. However, it has continued many of the previous aspects, cutting some good parts. Therefore, this program could not be new. And today, it has not been able to accept the change brought about by the Gen Z movement. The brand that this government had created has diminished. This is just a suggestion to the government. Honourable Chairperson, I would like to draw your attention to my amendment. And at this time, the guidance specified by the constitution for transforming the country and achieving sustainable goals has been completely rejected. Words like democracy, republic, federalism, and socialism have not been included. And in which direction this transformation is heading is unclear. Therefore, I would like to state that this economic policy is a directionless economic program. And there are good things here. Tax exemptions have been provided for entrepreneurs and the middle class. But it has never recognized the common people, the poor, the working class, and the landless. And

It did not solve the problem of the unitary governance system. Although it was said to be so, it has not recognized the three tiers of government. While digitizing the economy and providing IT-based services is good, the policy and programs did not come to make the economy self-reliant. And the self-reliance of farmers, the production of farmers, as the honorable members said before, it has again led to a situation where production has to be dumped in the market, dairies have to be closed, and farmers have to protest on the streets for not receiving payment for their produce. And there are no programs that would make the youth stay in the country, even though they were mentioned. Today, no alternative employment management program has been introduced for the more than 2 million unemployed youth. Today, no such investment has been made in sectors like education and health as required, and no such programs have come in the policy. Although it was said to improve the quality of community schools, no programs have been introduced, and the children there, especially the children, are facing injustice and oppression regarding their midday meals and the teachers. Such things have not been mentioned anywhere here. And today there are 21 national pride projects. Nothing has been said about these projects in this policy and program. There are many projects like Nijgadh, and people are suffering from inflation every day. But the government has not brought any policy or program to manage this inflation and provide alternatives. And this government is very confused and has not spoken about the three-pillar economy. The policy of giving concessions to the powerful and punishing the common people needs to be reminded. While it is right to make civil and other employees accountable, to provide them with easy service, and to make them accountable to the public, and it is right for them to remain neutral. However, how can the abolition of trade unions, which they are organizing, be included in this economic policy? I want to state that this is completely unconstitutional and also a violation of human rights. And by including everyone, all sectors, women, Dalits, Janajatis, indigenous people, the lower class, and youth, the vision of social justice and a welfare state is not seen in this policy and program. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri. Time 7 minutes. (19:52 hrs) After this, Honorable Member Mahanta Thakur. Honorable Shri Ram Kumari Jhankri (Communist Party of Nepal, UML): Honorable Chairperson, while discussing the policy and program for the fiscal year 2083/084, I was reminded of an essay I read in childhood. Generally, there was a small paragraph in an essay that said, "We ordinary people are humans born of an era. Many people are born in an era, and we are such people. But in the world, there are some epoch-making men, some powers, who give birth to an era." There was an expectation that a power would emerge and give birth to an era, defeating our party and other old democratic parties, in the elections of the 21st of this month, in the words of Chandra Dai, the democratic parties. When the policy and program were reviewed, it seemed like a continuation of the old program, and it is a continuation of the old program. The points have been reduced. But the previous programs have been repeated, with the sentences slightly compressed and condensed. Therefore, there is not much to comment on. Now, a party that has come with such a huge mandate had an opportunity to make a departure in Nepali society. The public has given this opportunity to all political parties at one time or another in the past. In 2015, to the Nepali Congress, in 2048, again to the Nepali Congress, then in 2064, to the then CPN (Maoist Centre), in '74 to the CPN, the CPN including CPN-UML, and now in 2082 to Rastriya Swatantra Party. However, if the public's desire for change, desire for transformation, is thwarted by traditional ways, and remains in the status quo, then no one will address the public's aspirations, and this program shows the same continuity. Therefore, since it is a copy of the old program, there is no need to say more. But political parties have changed. A political party has a departure perspective. When a captain sits at the helm of a ship, they need navigation to know where to go. The navigator shows them. Which path will they take to move forward? To achieve these things, to achieve what, when asked which path to take, they have taken points on good governance and economic development. Good governance today means first strangling the driving force of the private sector economy and then sleeping. Good governance is here. First strangle, then sleep. If you reverse this and look at it, I would like to suggest to the government whether it is better to sleep after strangling or to strangle after sleeping. Then, instead of intimidating everyone, creating an environment and encouragement for people to work. This is what is happening, and where will they go with this work? What will they do? There is nothing. Governing by intimidating people immediately and using a kind of coercive power. I am talking about coercive power repeatedly because this is a way of governing by intimidating, harassing, and threatening people. What is happening will not show a new path. Therefore, I am also saddened by this, that this government has come with such great public expectations. For this reason, it has many advantages compared to other governments formed in the past based on coalitions and party agreements, and they have not paid attention to these advantages. Now, in this context, talking about economic development, what is the pattern and structure of today's economy? What is being sought? What is the philosophy being sought? From what path? What is our investment method for 7% growth? What is the mechanism? What reforms will we make? What are they saying? They are delivering. We will deliver. We will deliver good governance. Delivery is not just about issuing passports, citizenship certificates, licenses, land ownership certificates. It is also about ensuring the right to life for all people. It is also the right to life for those who are marginalized from all these rights. How has the policy and program addressed this? When talking about development infrastructure, I am talking about loan assistance. We have had many discussions about the mistakes we have made throughout history, that loan assistance was used in unproductive sectors, but what are our game-changer programs to move towards productivity? The policy did not navigate. It did not do that, and now it is only about what has been heard. Talking about infrastructure, even about cities, the process of digging, building, digging, rebuilding, for which the city's ugly structure and the government's investment in soil and mud have been wasted for a long time, utility corridors were so important, the law was drafted during our time, and its commitment is not visible. Today, the work of laying wires for the beauty of the city is being done. Those are the most dangerous, and if they are damaged again at any time, it is a process of digging. We don't even have corridors. Irrigation has been mentioned. What is the guarantee that the cost of underground water irrigation and lift irrigation will yield returns according to the cost? This has come before. Will the returns match the investment or not? Should we spend loan assistance of one hundred thousand rupees, which yields even ten thousand rupees in income, there or not? And have you spoken at all about prioritizing roads and highways? Let's classify the roads that are open year-round. If the government also thinks about doing a model project with joint local, provincial, and federal government co-investment, it seems like some good things might happen. Therefore, regarding irrigation, this government has the opportunity to review the land use law. Will this review be done to control the tendency of land being plotted before irrigation projects are completed? And should the language be changed from 'those who own land will get it'? The state has an obligation to fulfill the fundamental rights of the constitution and our international commitments, our national and international commitments. Beyond that, if the government commits to increasing Nepal's GDP size, increasing income, increasing per capita income, and increasing our growth based on returns, then perhaps this is the opportunity, and this opportunity will be gone tomorrow morning when the sun rises. Therefore, I sincerely request this government to utilize this opportunity and wish them good luck. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Mahanta Thakur. Time 5 minutes. (12:00 hrs) After this, Honorable Member Dharmendra Paswan. Honorable Shri Mahanta Thakur (Loktantrik Samajwadi Party, Nepal): Honorable Chairperson, the two main issues of the ENJI movement were good governance and corruption, but bulldozers are being run against the landless. What should that be called? Good governance? So, this is the definition of good governance. It is approved by the public, even if the results seem unusual. Yes, therefore, we have accepted it. Therefore, whatever definition you give to anything, we will accept it. The same applies to corruption. What is corruption? Misuse of government money is corruption. That seems fine. But if service recipients give something willingly after receiving their service, what is that called? Is that also corruption? Now, money laundering has already arrived. Now, who has been purified, has the body also been purified? Let's see what happened to the body. The Prime Minister came yesterday, he was not wearing a cap. But whenever something happens, in Kathmandu, the doors used to be a bit low. So, it was difficult to bring furniture etc. Therefore, they used to fill sacks with straw and make them into cushions, and then put real straw on top. After a few days, a strange kind of bug would emerge from it, that's the bug. Now, he was doing the same thing yesterday. Is that bug the PM? Or if he wears a cap, it won't be visible. He wasn't wearing a cap. Therefore, this bug PM seems to be the case now, maybe it won't happen. Now comes the Marwari society. Is he infamous by name or what? Marwari. So, today they are caught, for money laundering or something, they say. Then they release them for two days, then catch them again. Houses are burned, looted. All these actions against him, on one hand, to improve the economic situation, to move forward, what capital has our Finance Minister asked for, we will also hear that. What is it? Domestic capital, foreign capital, public capital. Now, domestic capital is with our businessmen. Now, they are not allowed to invest. They are put in jail. Now

They are participating. Let's hear what Chaudhary has to say. Many names have already left the country. They could not bear the hardship here. And they have made great contributions to our society. In education, health, and enterprise, the Marwari community has made a significant contribution. If we drive them away, and whatever little we have, our domestic capital, is also scared. Where will investment come from? Of course, migrants are also Nepalis. But they are living abroad. Their contribution is also visible. But if we count here, no capital will come. So, how will the development you envision happen? That is also something we need to think about. We have various types of tenders here, along with judicial tenders. Why do I use this word? Because even now, our colleagues, for six months, regarding the draft of the constitution, the current constitution... (Time expired.) When I myself was the Vice-Chairman of the National Planning Commission, the then Prime Minister considered it appropriate to upgrade at that time. Because there are three criteria for this upgrade. One is GDP per capita, related to the economy, economic per capita income. Another is related to economic risks, economic vulnerability, and the third is human resources or human assets. This includes subjects like education, health, and nutrition. Overall, based on about 12-13 indicators across three pillars...

It is in practice and the assessment that takes place every three years, if we pass two consecutive ones, we become eligible for an upgrade. At that time, I suggested that without a strong economy, an upgrade based on non-economic indicators would not be sustainable and could be reversed later. Therefore, I had advised against rushing to graduate and risking a reversal due to external shocks, as our upgrade would not be mature enough. Subsequently, it was postponed to 2021. (19:01 hrs) Honorable Finance Minister Mr. Swarnim Wagle:- Honorable Chairperson of the National Assembly,
I stand here today as the Finance Minister of a government formed with an unprecedented mandate from the people through a general election, based on the foundation of the movement and sacrifice of the change-seeking youth who aspire for a capable, just, and prosperous Nepal. On this occasion, I respectfully remember the martyrs who sacrificed their lives for political freedom, civil rights, and judicial prosperity in this esteemed house, and I express solidarity and wish for the speedy recovery of the injured and affected citizens during the movement.

We are in the process of budget formulation, keeping in mind good governance and justice, employment-oriented economic growth, and quality public services and equal opportunities. Remaining steadfast towards the Constitution of Nepal, democratic values, and the core ideals of good governance, the current government is moving towards establishing policy stability, institutional strengthening, and a result-oriented governance system with the slogan "Establishing Order".

With the objective of realizing this very resolve, I present the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill for the fiscal year 2083/084. Initially, I present five guiding principles of the Appropriation Bill, 2083.

(a) Dividend of Good Governance
We will establish good governance as a tangible benefit for citizens, in terms of state legitimacy, service efficiency, and economic equity. The rule of law, institutional efficiency, and the supremacy of public integrity will be the starting point for guaranteeing good governance. We will implement a series of governance reforms to ensure that the direct benefits of good governance are felt in the daily lives of citizens by making the state accountable and technology-friendly.

The upcoming budget will focus on ensuring fast and reliable public services that save citizens' time, labor, and cost. Through administrative reforms based on integrated digital good governance, we will end delays, hassles, and unwanted intermediaries in service delivery.

We will review the state's policies, laws, and regulatory arrangements extensively, freeing public institutions from illegal occupation and exploitative practices. We will make the investigation and prosecution system against money laundering, revenue leakage, misuse of public resources, and organized crime a result-oriented campaign against corruption.

(b) Restructuring of the Economy
Achieving high, broad, and rapid economic growth and creating sustainable employment will be the main goal of economic restructuring. The upcoming budget will transform the consumption-based economy into an investment-based and production-oriented economy. We will advance a "new phase of economic reform" based on the expansion of economic opportunities, promotion of entrepreneurship, ensuring a competitive environment, and productive mobilization of financial resources. We will strengthen the investment-friendly economic environment through predictable management of balanced public finance.

We will restore the confidence of the private sector and remove obstacles in business and enterprise. We will strengthen a social market economy oriented towards equality by ending unhealthy competition, syndicates, cartels, and monopolies. We will encourage production and innovation by making the tax system simple and just. We will promote the digital economy, service exports, clean energy, and high value-added agriculture as drivers of economic transformation. We will make radical improvements in international-standard air services, telecommunications, and logistics infrastructure to reduce the structural economic burden inherent in Nepal's landlocked reality. We will adopt temporary protective measures to enhance the competitiveness of import-substituting industries. The security of private property will be the responsibility of the state.

(c) Integrated Infrastructure for Connectivity
Connectivity reduces the distance not only between geography and settlements but also between production, markets, services, and opportunities, thereby strengthening economic and social interrelationships. We will contribute to economic dynamism and social integration by expanding connectivity through large-scale infrastructure construction.

We will develop road, air, energy, urban, and digital infrastructure with an integrated approach. We will strengthen institutional coordination by keeping infrastructure within the discipline of time, cost, and quality.

We will ensure the appropriate mobilization of capital, technology, and managerial capacity for balanced development so that the benefits reach all regions and communities of the country. We will expand digital public infrastructure to take economic activities, service delivery, and national connectivity to a new level.

We will adopt the concept of climate-resilient infrastructure development, taking into account environmental balance and disaster risks, climate change, and climate change. The relationship between conservation, utilization, and future security of natural resources will be balanced.

(d) Universal Social Upliftment and Expansion of the Middle Class
We will develop capable human capital by ensuring equal access to quality education, health, nutrition, and skills. We will build a reliable foundation of social security for individuals who require state protection. We will expand the middle class by guaranteeing economic mobility and social security. We will promote agriculture and micro, small, and medium enterprises and provide practical and employment-oriented education to develop a skilled workforce. We will mobilize appropriate financial resources to link innovation, entrepreneurship, and startup culture with production and employment.

We will link the education system with production, entrepreneurship, innovation, and the labor market. We will increase state investment in technical and vocational education and emphasize employment-centered education. Through the restructuring of health insurance and social security systems, we will strengthen citizens' access to health services and financial security. We will take concrete steps to improve the living standards of all Nepalis.

We will link social mobility (upward mobility) not only with representation but also with economic opportunities and dignified participation.

(e) Strengthening of Soft Power
The government will strengthen balanced foreign relations based on mutual benefit, national self-respect, and sovereign interests, and utilize soft power for economic prosperity. We will expand Nepal's international presence, credibility, and influence through the integrated use of economic diplomacy, cultural identity, technology, and tourism. We will increase economic benefits by developing mature relationships with neighboring and friendly countries and international organizations.

We will mobilize the savings, skills, and capital of Nepalis living abroad as a driving force for national development, along with domestic capital, technology, and entrepreneurship. We will facilitate the connection of the expertise of non-resident Nepalis with the national economy. We will make legal reforms to link economic diplomacy with investment, technology transfer, export expansion, and mobilization of international capital.

Honorable Chairperson, now I present the priorities of the Appropriation Bill.

(a) Legal and Institutional Reforms and Optimal Use of Information Technology for Service Delivery
The budget will prioritize the creation of a strong state structure through a cooperative federal governance system. We will focus the federal government on policy formulation, research, national standard setting, and transformative projects, while the provincial level will focus on coordination, provincial planning, and service facilitation.

We will restructure them as dynamic bridges. We will strive to ensure financial resources and institutional capacity, strengthening local levels as implementation units of the state. Specifically, we will connect education, health, agriculture, tourism, and basic service delivery with local potential. We will review laws related to investment, the financial sector, and public service delivery and implement a "one-door, time-bound, and digital" administrative system. We will end dual roles by clearly dividing responsibilities between regulatory and implementation bodies. We will integrate processes from business registration to permits, tax administration, payments, and regulation into a digital system.

Removing legal, procedural, and institutional obstacles seen in the implementation of large projects is a government priority. We will implement a performance agreement with project chiefs, ensuring a fixed tenure, clear responsibilities, and a results-based evaluation system. We will simplify processes related to forests, environment, land acquisition, public procurement, and construction materials, and implement strategic projects in a "mission mode." We will implement strict regulatory measures against conflicts of interest, cartels, and monopolistic practices. We will implement a risk-based audit system for monitoring public procurement, revenue administration, service delivery, and policy-making processes. We will make the asset details and expenditure systems of individuals in public positions transparent, thereby re-establishing public trust in the state.

Our priority is to build a modern administration that provides "more service with less" and end the situation where citizens have to go through lines, hassle, and unnecessary intermediaries to access public services. We will make the civil and public administration professional, neutral, capable, motivated, and results-oriented. We will expand "single service centers" that provide essential public services seven days a week.

Transformation of public administration based on data, technology, and artificial intelligence is a government priority. We will develop an integrated database and interlinked government system based on the principle of "one-time data entry for all services" using the national identity card. We will provide services such as citizenship, business registration, tax, health, education, social security, land, banking, and other public services through the "Citizen App" and an integrated digital platform.

(b) Re-prioritization of Sectoral Sources of Economic Growth
The upcoming budget will adopt a policy of re-prioritizing limited public resources and private investment towards sectors with high returns, employment, and value addition. We will develop agriculture, energy, tourism, information technology, and service sectors as drivers of economic growth, transforming the economy from consumption-based imports to one based on production, productivity, innovation, and exports. Maximizing the utilization of capital assets that have been created but not fully utilized, as well as the production capacity of the private sector, will be a major priority of the government.

Systematically strengthening the interrelationship between agricultural production, processing, storage, distribution, marketing, and consumption, and restructuring the agricultural sector is another government priority. We will promote agriculture as a basis for rural prosperity, food security, employment generation, and import substitution. We will adopt a "commercial agriculture model" by protecting small farmers and creating economies of scale in production. We will connect farmers to markets, technology, finance, insurance, processing, and price assurance through cooperatives, producer companies, contract farming, and agri-business groups. We will expand "production clusters" in potential areas, integrating irrigation, roads, cold storage, testing laboratories, seed-fertilizer-pesticide services, and processing industries as a package. We will implement a minimum support price for food grains and make high-value crops, animal husbandry, medicinal herbs, and agro-forestry systems export-oriented. The subsidy system will be production-oriented. We will connect agriculture to a competitive, modern, and green economy through farmer records, market intelligence, agricultural insurance, and concessional finance and mechanization. We will promote forest-based industries, medicinal herb processing, carbon trading, biodiversity conservation, and climate-resilient production systems.

We will make physical infrastructure development a strong foundation for economic transformation. Through the "Investment Express" policy, we will simplify and expedite the approval and implementation process for industries, investments, and infrastructure projects. We will develop the mining and mineral sector and increase the productive use of domestic resources. We will encourage private sector investment in green hydrogen, energy storage, and clean industrial technologies.

We will mobilize long-term capital by focusing public investment on transformative projects and through alternative development finance, infrastructure bonds, offshore green bonds, diaspora capital, and public-private partnerships. We will identify non-commercial investment areas focused on production for institutional savings and welfare funds that have not been utilized. We will focus foreign aid and loans on national priorities and high-return projects.

We will enhance financial discipline and private sector confidence by restructuring public enterprises, managing assets, and through monetization and effective public management. We will build long-term capital by expanding institutional investors in the capital market in line with international standards, developing debt and bond markets, and providing innovative financial instruments.

With the objective of transforming Nepal into an "economy that creates high value without weight," we will promote the export of software, cloud services, data centers, AI computation, cybersecurity, and digital services. We will provide legal recognition to remote work, digital nomads, international payment systems, and digital enterprises, developing Nepal as a regional "tech hub." We will integrate "Startup Nepal" and national entrepreneurship and innovation programs.

We will develop urbanization and regional connectivity as new poles of economic growth. We will qualitatively expand religious, cultural, health-related, adventure, and community-based tourism. We will strengthen rural-urban economic linkages through economic corridors.

(c) Mobilization of Multi-sectoral Resources for Physical Infrastructure
Completing transformative projects that have been pending for a long time is another major priority of the government. We will focus limited resources on completing pending projects and high-return projects rather than adding new ones. We will expedite the construction of ongoing energy production, transmission, and distribution projects and advance preparatory projects. We will increase energy consumption, expand regional energy trade, and promote energy-based industries. We will provide financial concessions and facilitate investment for the development of renewable energy-based industries. We will expand irrigation in the Terai-Madhesh region based on underground water resources in areas not served by irrigation. We will implement lift irrigation and restore traditional irrigation systems in the hilly and mountainous regions. We will complete large irrigation projects as soon as possible.

To enhance national economic integration and market access, we will complete the remaining sections of strategic road projects such as Pushpalal, Hulaki, North-South Corridor, and Kathmandu-Terai-Madhesh Expressway. We will allocate budget to expedite the construction of roads being built to connect various municipalities from the main highways. We will collaborate with the private sector in the construction of subways, flyovers, underpasses, and overpasses. To support industrial and export promotion, we will develop economic corridors, dry ports, warehouses, cold chains, and multi-modal logistics infrastructure.

We will link urbanization with economic growth, service delivery, and improvement of living standards. We will prioritize mass transit systems in major cities, including the Kathmandu Valley. We will promote a circular urban economy by developing integrated solid waste management, sewage treatment, and reuse systems. We will strengthen Melamchi and other national importance drinking water projects and ensure regular and safe water supply.

We will develop tourism circuits based on Lumbini-Boudha, Janakpur-Ramayan, Himalayas, and nature. We will stimulate local economies through the development of new trekking routes, homestays, cultural destinations, and service centers. By fully operationalizing airports, effectively implementing aviation safety standards, and restructuring Nepal Airlines Corporation, we will develop Nepal as a safe regional tourism hub.

We will develop digital public infrastructure as a basis for economic competitiveness. We will expand data centers, G-Cloud, high-speed internet, cybersecurity, and digital payment infrastructure.

(d) Social System for Equality of Opportunity
We will restructure the education system from basic to higher levels to make it free from political interference, competitive, and linked to the labor market. At all levels of education, we will prioritize quality learning over mere expansion. We will advance the education system in a direction that supports the country's economic transformation.

School education will be oriented towards critical thinking, providing basic and essential learning to all children. Technical and vocational education will be developed as a major engine for economic growth, employment, and productivity, while higher education will be the foundation for capability, knowledge, research, and innovation. We will improve the quality of public education through school mapping, school sector planning, common quality standards, teacher-student ratio adjustment, and school classification. We will bring all public and private schools under common standards of minimum learning and inclusion. We will implement a system based on merit, performance, and professional development, keeping teachers and headmasters at the center of educational reform.

We will make higher education research-oriented, competitive, and innovation-focused, strengthening collaboration between universities, industries, and research institutions. We will establish a "National Research and Innovation Fund" for research and development (R&D) and provide long-term financial support for research and innovation related to science, technology, health, energy, agriculture, artificial intelligence, and digital transformation. We will connect sports to national pride, health, tourism, and the overall economy by professionalizing the sports sector and enhancing international competitiveness.

We will develop an integrated health service system with necessary manpower, medicines, equipment, and infrastructure by implementing a "minimum standard" for basic health services. We will prioritize the expansion of basic hospitals at the local level and health service access in rural and remote areas. We will restructure health insurance and health-related social security programs to make them citizen-friendly. We will prioritize disease prevention, mental health, nutrition, non-communicable disease control, telehealth services, and strengthening the public health system. We will scientifically and systematically promote Ayurveda, yoga, meditation, and alternative treatment methods. We will strengthen the quality regulation of private health institutions. We will provide community-based care for senior citizens, persons with disabilities, and chronically ill citizens.

Expand the economy. Restructure the social security program as a basis for equity, targeted protection, the state's economic capacity, and social mobility. Expand entrepreneurship opportunities targeting workers returning from foreign employment. Implement an apprenticeship and employment promotion program based on the concept of "earning while learning." Gradually transform the informal sector into the formal economy, bringing workers into social insurance and labor protection. Restructure the cooperative sector, financial sector, and savings sector as a basis for the productive economy, developing a regulated and member-centric system based on trust, discipline, and scope. Address the problems of savers in the long term through regulatory reforms. Reducing structural inequality, exclusion, and imbalance of opportunity is a major responsibility of the state. High priority will be given to expanding equal access to public services for backward regions, marginalized communities, and those deprived of opportunities. Structural discrimination historically faced by the Dalit community will be ended, and targeted interventions will be strengthened. The remaining tasks of the peace process will be brought to conclusion to ensure justice for victims. The identification of landless and squatters, secure housing, land ownership, and livelihood opportunities will be strengthened. The transformation of historically deprived regions such as Karnali, Madhesh, and Sudurpaschim, which are disconnected from the mainstream of development, is a top priority of the state. These regions will be developed not just as recipients of grants or relief, but as strategic centers for national potential, agriculture, water resources, tourism, culture, entrepreneurship, and human capital development. (d) Diversification of multidimensional international relations. Nepal's sovereignty, territorial integrity, self-respect, and national interest will be paramount in developing balanced, independent, and results-oriented foreign relations. Foreign policy will be made a vehicle for economic transformation, emphasizing the qualitative expansion of foreign investment, technology transfer, energy trade, tourism, exports, and foreign employment. Diplomatic efforts will be made to establish Nepal as an attractive center for information technology, education, health services, green energy, and digital services. The "Diaspora Partnership" for national development will be strengthened to mobilize the capital, knowledge, skills, technology, and international networks of Nepali communities living abroad. Legal and institutional reforms will be advanced to facilitate investment, financial participation, and innovation by non-resident Nepalis in the national development campaign. Access to international financial institutions, climate finance, technology, and innovation will be expanded, and Nepal will be meaningfully integrated with the world economy. Honorable Chairperson, finally, the budget for the upcoming fiscal year 2083/084 will address the country's existing economic challenges and lay a sustainable foundation for a prosperous Nepal. The principles and priorities of the presented Appropriation Bill focus on employment-centric economic growth, structural reform, digital transformation, and good governance. It contains a commitment to bring qualitative improvement in the living standards of citizens through the restoration of private sector confidence, the creation of an investment-friendly environment, and technology-friendly public service delivery. I expect that a thorough discussion will take place among the honorable members on the principles and priorities presented today before this respected house. I express my commitment to accept the suggestions received from this discussion as a guide for the budget formulation of the upcoming fiscal year. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson, with the permission of the Chairperson, I present to this respected house the proposal that the Appropriation Bill for the fiscal year 2083/084, excluding tax proposals, be discussed in the house. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, regarding the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill for the fiscal year 2083/084, I inform the honorable members that discussions will be held in the National Assembly meeting on May 18 and 19, 2083 (Baisakh 4 and 5), and the honorable Finance Minister will respond to the questions raised during the discussion on May 20, 2083 (Baisakh 6). Honorable members, regarding the discussion on the Appropriation Bill for the fiscal year 2083/084, excluding tax proposals, the discussion will focus only on the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill. I inform the honorable members who wish to participate in the discussion to provide their names, based on party representation, to the Management Division of the National Assembly one day before the discussion day. Honorable members, I direct the Ministry of Finance to be present and take notes on the issues that honorable members will raise regarding the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill for the fiscal year 2083/084. Honorable members, the next meeting of the National Assembly will be held on Monday, May 20, 2083, at 1:15 PM, and this meeting is adjourned. (Thereafter, the next meeting will be held on Monday, May 20, 2083, at 1:15 PM, and this meeting is adjourned.) Adjourned: 7:26 PM.

sections.summary_en: Honourable Member Krishna Bahadur Rokaya raised concerns about road safety following recent fatal accidents, urging the government for plans to prevent recurrence. Honourable Member Padam Bahadur Pariyar spoke about the plight of a disabled individual seeking personal assistant services and euthanasia. Honourable Member Puja Chaudhary highlighted the dire living conditions of landless squatters and urged for proper management before demolition. Honourable Member Rukmini Koirala proposed amending the Cooperative Act regarding repayment obligations. Honourable Member Renu Chand requested easier pedestrian access to Singha Durbar. Honourable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota addressed the issues of landless, unorganized settlers, and the poor, demanding transparent identification and basic services. Honourable Member Bishnu Bahadur Bishwakarma demanded strict action against those responsible for the death of a Dalit youth in custody. Honourable Member Shrikrishna Prasad Adhikari criticized the government's demolition of squatter settlements without management and highlighted their poor living conditions. Honourable Member Savitri Malla critiqued the government's policy and program for lacking novelty and failing to address key issues like petroleum price hikes and gas production.

They argue that the policy lacks a clear vision for economic self-reliance and social justice, and instead perpetuates old programs with minor changes. The speaker also raises concerns about the abolition of trade unions and the government's approach to economic development, emphasizing the need for a clear strategy and investment in productive sectors.

The speaker criticizes the government's approach to good governance, arguing it creates fear rather than encouragement, and questions the philosophy and strategy for economic development, particularly regarding investment and reforms. sections.summary_en: The speaker discusses climate change finance, advocating for direct allocation to local municipalities and criticizing administrative waste. They also propose prioritizing storage-based hydropower, expanding transmission lines, and promoting electricity load industries. The speaker further suggests focusing on religious tourism, citing Ayodhya as an example, and emphasizes the need for concrete steps in the policy and program. Additionally, they address the issue of reverse brain drain, advocating for policies that retain skilled youth and utilize their expertise for national development, rather than relying solely on remittances. The speaker also critiques the 'Digital Nepal' vision, highlighting the digital divide and advocating for student-centric e-learning initiatives and the establishment of a National Digital Equity Fund. Finally, they stress the importance of the constitution, urging the government to accept their amendments for economic growth, climate justice, and digital equity.

He acknowledges the prioritization of economic reform, infrastructure, energy, agriculture, tourism, and digital services as welcome but stresses the need for tangible results over mere assurances, citing past implementation failures. He highlights the challenges faced by farmers despite policy mentions of price support, the continued emigration of youth seeking opportunities, and the weak state of rural education and technological access. The speaker also notes the gap between stated commitments to good governance and public experience, and persistent issues with project delays and ineffective budget spending. He further points out the absence of clear policies for national pride projects, import-oriented economy, strengthening federalism, utilizing returning youth, and disaster management, urging for a refinement of the policy and program to focus on citizens' rights, social justice, and federalism.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The government plans to restructure infrastructure as dynamic bridges, strengthen local governance, and implement digital administrative systems. Key priorities include removing legal and procedural obstacles for large projects, simplifying processes for forest, environment, and land acquisition, and implementing strict regulations against monopolies. The focus is on modernizing public administration for efficiency and transparency, and transforming it with data, technology, and AI through integrated databases and digital platforms like the Citizen App.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The upcoming budget will re-prioritize public and private investment towards high-return sectors like agriculture, energy, tourism, and IT, shifting from import-based consumption to production and export-driven growth. The government aims to maximize the utilization of existing capital assets and private sector production capacity. Restructuring the agricultural sector is a priority, focusing on strengthening the value chain from production to consumption, promoting commercial agriculture models, and supporting farmers through cooperatives and technology.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Physical infrastructure development is a foundation for economic transformation, with policies to expedite project approval and implementation. The mining sector will be developed, and private investment in green technologies encouraged. Long-term capital will be mobilized through various financing mechanisms, focusing public investment on transformative projects. Nepal aims to become a "value-creating economy" by promoting digital services exports and developing as a regional tech hub.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Urbanization and regional connectivity will be developed as growth poles, with qualitative expansion of tourism. The government prioritizes completing long-pending transformative infrastructure projects, especially in energy and irrigation, to enhance national economic integration and market access. Strategic road projects will be completed, and private sector collaboration sought for urban infrastructure like subways and flyovers.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Urbanization will be linked to economic growth and improved living standards, with priorities on mass transit, waste management, and water supply. Tourism circuits will be developed, and Nepal positioned as a regional tourism hub through airport modernization and airline restructuring. Digital public infrastructure, including data centers and high-speed internet, will be expanded.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The education system will be restructured to be competitive and labor-market-aligned, prioritizing quality learning and supporting economic transformation. School education will focus on critical thinking, while technical/vocational and higher education will drive economic growth, employment, research, and innovation. A "National Research and Innovation Fund" will be established to support R&D in key sectors.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Basic health services will be standardized with integrated systems, prioritizing access in rural areas and restructuring health insurance. Disease prevention, mental health, and public health systems will be strengthened. Traditional and alternative medicine will be promoted scientifically, and the quality of private health institutions regulated. Community-based care will be provided for vulnerable groups.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The session focused on economic development, social security reforms, and international relations. The Finance Minister presented the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill for FY 2083/084, emphasizing employment-centric growth, structural reforms, and digital transformation. Discussions on the bill were scheduled for subsequent dates.
